cards.front: A {{c1::population}} is all the members of one species that live in the same area at the same time.
cards.quote: A population is all the members of one species that live in the same area at the same time.
cards.section: Explain: who lives together and what holds them back

cards.front: On one creek that flows into the Chesapeake Bay, the blue crabs, fish, clams and marsh grass together are a community, not a population. Why?
cards.back: A population is one species only. A community is all the populations of different species in an area that interact.
cards.quote: The crabs, fish, clams and marsh grass of the creek form a community.
cards.section: Explain: who lives together and what holds them back

cards.front: An {{c1::ecosystem}} is a community together with its nonliving surroundings, such as water, mud, air and sunlight.
cards.quote: An ecosystem is a community together with its nonliving surroundings, such as water, mud, air and sunlight.
cards.section: Explain: who lives together and what holds them back

cards.front: A {{c1::biotic factor}} is a living part of the environment, such as predators, food, competitors and disease.
cards.quote: A biotic factor is a living part of the environment, such as predators, food, competitors and disease.
cards.section: Explain: who lives together and what holds them back

cards.front: An {{c1::abiotic factor}} is a nonliving part of the environment, such as temperature, moisture, air, salinity (salt level) and pH.
cards.quote: An abiotic factor is a nonliving part of the environment, such as temperature, moisture, air, salinity (salt level) and pH.
cards.section: Explain: who lives together and what holds them back

cards.front: Cold water and low salt in a creek both limit blue crabs. Are they biotic or abiotic factors, and how can you tell?
cards.back: Abiotic. Both are nonliving conditions of the environment (temperature and salinity). A predator or a disease would be biotic because it is living.
cards.quote: An abiotic factor is a nonliving part of the environment, such as temperature, moisture, air, salinity (salt level) and pH.
cards.section: Explain: who lives together and what holds them back

cards.front: A {{c1::limiting factor}} is anything that keeps a population from growing larger.
cards.quote: A limiting factor is anything that keeps a population from growing larger.
cards.section: Explain: who lives together and what holds them back

cards.front: What is competition between individuals in a population?
cards.back: It happens when individuals need the same limited resource, such as food or a hiding place.
cards.quote: Competition happens when individuals need the same limited resource, such as food or a hiding place.
cards.section: Explain: who lives together and what holds them back

cards.front: How do larger blue crabs act as a biotic limiting factor on young blue crabs?
cards.back: They are predators. Adult blue crabs eat young crabs, so fewer young crabs survive.
cards.quote: Adult blue crabs eat young crabs, so fewer young survive.
cards.section: Explain: who lives together and what holds them back

cards.front: Ten bacteria land in a dish of fresh food, and each one splits in two every 30 minutes. How many bacteria are there after four steps, and is the number added each step the same or larger?
cards.back: 10 to 20 to 40 to 80 to 160, so 160 after four steps. The number added grows each step (10, 20, 40, 80), though each step is the same fraction (doubling). This is exponential growth.
cards.quote: After one step there are 20, then 40, 80, 160 and 320.

cards.front: Exponential growth can happen in a small population. Why can it not last?
cards.back: It needs plentiful resources. As the population grows, food runs short and waste builds up.
cards.quote: It can happen while a population is small and resources are plentiful, but it cannot last: food runs short and waste builds up.

cards.front: What shape is exponential growth on a graph, and how does the simplest limited-growth curve differ from it?
cards.back: Exponential growth is J-shaped. In the simplest limited-growth model the curve bends into an S shape and approaches carrying capacity.
cards.quote: In the simplest limited-growth model, the curve bends into an S shape and approaches carrying capacity; real populations often move around that level.

cards.front: The {{c1::carrying capacity}} is the largest population the environment can support over time with its resources and challenges.
cards.quote: which levels off near the carrying capacity, the largest population the environment can support over time with its resources and challenges

cards.front: In the initial growth part of a growth curve, why does a small population add only a few individuals?
cards.back: Few individuals are present to have young.
cards.quote: A small population adds only a few individuals because few are present to have young.

cards.front: What is true of births and deaths in a population at steady state, and what is this balance called?
cards.back: Births and deaths are about equal if few individuals move in or out. The balance, kept by ongoing change, is a dynamic equilibrium.
cards.quote: Births and deaths are about equal if few individuals move in or out.

cards.front: In a steady state the balance kept by ongoing change is called a {{c1::dynamic equilibrium}}.
cards.quote: This balance, kept by ongoing change, is a dynamic equilibrium.

cards.front: In the five-part growth curve, are decline and extinction required stages for every population?
cards.back: No. They are possible later outcomes if conditions get worse, not required stages.
cards.quote: Decline and extinction are possible later outcomes, not required stages of every curve.

cards.front: Blue crabs vanish from one creek but remain elsewhere in the Bay. Is the species extinct?
cards.back: No. The creek population has undergone local extinction, but the species still lives in other populations.
cards.quote: When a population in one place reaches zero, it has undergone local extinction, which is different from extinction of a whole species.

cards.front: In a model population with limited growth, carrying capacity stays the same but the growth rate is raised. Does the population settle higher, or reach about the same level sooner?
cards.back: About the same level, sooner. In this simple model, the growth rate changes the trip, while carrying capacity sets the level approached.
cards.quote: In this simple model, the growth rate changes the trip, while carrying capacity sets the level approached.
cards.section: Explore: grow a population, then add limits

cards.front: What is the difference between density-dependent and density-independent limiting factors?
cards.back: Density-dependent factors (competition, disease, predators) get stronger as a population becomes crowded. Density-independent factors hit a population whatever its size.
cards.quote: Some limits get stronger as a population becomes crowded.
cards.section: Explain: which limits change with crowding

cards.front: A disease spreads through a crowded blue crab creek and through a sparse one. In which does it take the bigger share of crabs, and is it density-dependent?
cards.back: The crowded creek. Disease takes a bigger share of a crowded population, so it is density-dependent.
cards.quote: Disease is different: it takes a bigger share of a crowded population.
cards.section: Explain: which limits change with crowding

cards.front: A brief hard freeze kills many crabs, but the Bay's food, space and shelter stay the same. Does the freeze show that carrying capacity moved?
cards.back: No. A brief freeze lowers population size without, by itself, showing that carrying capacity moved.
cards.quote: Crabbing or a brief freeze lowers population size without, by itself, showing that carrying capacity moved.
cards.section: Explain: who lives together and what holds them back

cards.front: Two Bay creeks each lose half their crabs. In one, a hard freeze did it. In the other, shoreline building removed the marsh where young crabs hide for good. Which creek's crabs can be expected to grow back to the old level, and why?
cards.back: The freeze creek. Its food, space and shelter are unchanged, so carrying capacity is unchanged. Lost marsh is a lasting change in resources, so it can move carrying capacity down.
cards.quote: Lasting changes in resources or conditions can move carrying capacity. A short change in abundance does not prove that carrying capacity moved.

cards.front: Bay-wide winter survey estimates: 2024–2025 total 238 million, adult females 108 million; 2025–2026 total 349 million, adult females 81 million. By how much did each change, and did they move in the same direction?
cards.back: Total: 349 - 238 = +111 million. Adult females: 81 - 108 = -27 million. They moved in opposite directions.
cards.quote: From 2024–2025 to 2025–2026, did the total and the adult females change in the same direction? By how much did each change?

cards.front: Bay survey totals for eight winters (millions): 594, 405, 282, 227, 323, 317, 238, 349. Find the mean. Could that mean be the Bay's carrying capacity?
cards.back: Sum 2,735, mean about 342 million. No. The survey estimates abundance, so a mean of counts does not measure carrying capacity.
cards.quote: Find the mean total for the eight winters. Could that mean be the Bay's carrying capacity? Explain why or why not.

cards.front: What does the Bay's winter dredge survey estimate, and what can it not show?
cards.back: It estimates abundance (how many crabs). It does not measure carrying capacity, so it cannot show whether carrying capacity changed.
cards.quote: The survey estimates abundance; it does not measure carrying capacity, so it cannot show whether carrying capacity changed.

cards.front: In a duckweed experiment with several salt levels, the no-salt cups level off at the highest count and the saltier cups level off lower. What does this show about salt and carrying capacity?
cards.back: Salt lowers the carrying capacity in these cups. Saltier cups that also grow more slowly show salt slows growth.
cards.quote: If the saltier cups also level off lower, salt lowers the carrying capacity.

cards.front: In the duckweed salt experiment, why do all cups get the same pond water, plant food, light, temperature and starting number of fronds?
cards.back: These constants keep salt as the only difference between cups, so any change in growth can be linked to salt.
cards.quote: Constants: the same pond water and plant food, cup size, water volume, light, temperature and starting number of fronds (for example 10).

cards.front: In a lab study at 2 °C and a salinity of 5, only about 10% of blue crabs were alive after 40 days. Does this give the Bay's carrying capacity for crabs?
cards.back: No. It is one treatment's survival after 40 days. It shows an abiotic limit (cold, fresh water) on survival, not a carrying capacity for the whole Bay.
cards.quote: The 10% figure is one treatment's survival after 40 days, not a carrying capacity for the whole Bay.

cards.front: In a 2023 tank study with adult crabs present, how did the number of stand-in grass stems affect young blue crab survival?
cards.back: Young crabs survived better with more stand-in stems. The authors said the result still needs testing with real plants.
cards.quote: young blue crabs survived better when the tank held more wooden rods standing in for marsh grass stems, with adult crabs present as predators.
